# Acute abdomen

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Clinical problems > Acute abdomen*

[Original Article Link](/library/N50-4g)

---

## Summary

Acute abdomen refers to severe abdominal <u>pain</u> lasting for hours to a few days. The underlying pathology may be intraabdominal, thoracic, or systemic and may require urgent surgical intervention. The initial <u>approach to acute abdomen</u> should be to assess for immediately life-threatening causes (e.g., <u>ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm</u>, <u>bowel perforation</u>) by checking <u>vital signs</u>, performing a quick <u>physical examination</u>, and immediately conducting the appropriate focused diagnostic tests (e.g., abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>, <u>abdominal x-ray</u>). Once emergency causes have been ruled out, a thorough history and <u>physical examination</u> should be performed to narrow the differential diagnoses and guide further diagnostic workup and therapy. Causes of <u>chronic abdominal pain</u> are not addressed in this article.




See “<u>Blunt abdominal trauma</u>” and “<u>Penetrating abdominal trauma</u>” for details on traumatic causes of abdominal <u>pain</u>.




![Recognizing an acute abdomen](media/small_61000b87c5699.jpg)

Recognizing an acute abdomen

---

## Initial management

### Approach [[1]](/library/t9YX6r)




Evaluate and stabilize critically ill patients concurrently.




* Perform <u>ABCDE survey</u>: e.g., large-bore <u>IV access</u>, <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, <u>crossmatch</u> and <u>emergency transfusion</u> for suspected <u>hemorrhagic shock</u>.

* Establish <u>NPO</u> status.

* Perform a focused clinical evaluation, including <u>pelvic</u>, testicular, and rectal examination, if indicated.

* Perform targeted <u>diagnostic workup of acute abdomen</u>.

* Obtain urgent specialty consult as needed, e.g., general <u>surgery</u>, vascular <u>surgery</u>, urology, <u>OB/GYN</u> (see “Disposition” for details).

* Administer <u>supportive care for acute abdominal pain</u> as needed.

* Identify and treat the underlying cause.





> [!WARNING]
> Remember to consider gynecological causes such as <u>PID</u> and <u>pregnancy</u>-related conditions. [[2]](/library/2xcTDe0)




### Red flags for abdominal pain




The following <u>red flags</u> highlight conditions that can put patients at high risk for life-threatening causes of abdominal <u>pain</u> or misdiagnosis.




* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Age > 50 years

* <u>Immunocompromise</u> [[3]](/library/axcQEe0)

* Previous abdominal <u>surgery</u>  [[4]](/library/UxcbDe0)

* History of <u>CAD</u> and/or <u>atrial fibrillation</u>

* Unstable <u>vital signs</u>: <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>

* <u>Pain</u> characteristics

* Sudden onset of severe <u>pain</u>

* <u>Pain</u> that interrupts <u>sleep</u>

* <u>Pain out of proportion</u> to abdominal findings

* Accompanying symptoms

* <u>Bilious</u> <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Hematemesis</u>, <u>hematochezia</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u>

* Findings on examination

* Possible <u>peritoneal signs</u> 

* Guarding and/or rigidity (focal or diffused)

* <u>Rebound tenderness</u> (focal or diffused)

* Absent or tinkling <u>bowel sounds</u>

* Gross abdominal distention

* Irreducible, tender bulge on abdomen or groin





> [!WARNING]
> Abdominal <u>pain</u> accompanied by <u>hemodynamic instability</u> may indicate internal bleeding, perforated <u>viscus</u>, <u>necrotic</u> bowel, or <u>sepsis</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Maintain a high index of suspicion in <u>immunocompromised</u> and older patients, as they may present without <u>fever</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, or localized abdominal tenderness despite having an underlying life-threatening disease. [[3]](/library/axcQEe0)[[5]](/library/fxckDe0)




### Immediately life-threatening diagnoses




* <u>Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm</u>

* <u>Aortic dissection</u>

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Bowel perforation</u>

* <u>Mechanical bowel obstruction</u>

* <u>Acute mesenteric ischemia</u>

* <u>Acute pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Acute cholangitis</u>

* <u>Ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Delays in treatment of serious intraabdominal causes of acute abdominal <u>pain</u> can result in bowel <u>necrosis</u>, <u>sepsis</u>, <u>fistula</u> formation, and <u>death</u>.




### Disposition [[6]](/library/KnbU88)[[7]](/library/35YSPp)




* <u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients: Consider direct transfer to OR for patients needing emergency <u>surgery</u> or <u>ICU</u> admission.

* Underlying surgical pathology, intractable <u>nausea and vomiting</u>, and/or unremitting <u>pain</u>: inpatient admission

* Stable patients with inconclusive or negative diagnostic workup

* Extended observation in the ED with <u>serial abdominal examination</u>

* OR consider discharge with instructions and follow-up if the following criteria are met: :

* Resolution of <u>pain</u> and <u>nausea</u>

* Ability to tolerate oral intake

* Reassuring general appearance and <u>physical examination</u>

* Ability to adhere to discharge instructions.

* Examples of urgent consultations

* Vascular <u>surgery</u> for a ruptured or symptomatic <u>AAA</u>

* General <u>surgery</u> for <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients with a rigid abdomen

* Urology for <u>testicular torsion</u>

* <u>OB/GYN</u> for a <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>

---

## Diagnostics

The diagnostic workup should be guided by the <u>pretest probability</u> of the diagnoses under consideration. The following list includes some commonly used diagnostic tools that can help to diagnose or rule out possible etiologies in a patient with acute abdominal <u>pain</u>.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* <u>Blood gas analysis</u>

* <u>Lactate</u>

* <u>Troponin</u>

* Serum <u>glucose</u>

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Coagulation studies</u> (e.g., <u>INR</u>, <u>PT</u>)

* <u>BMP</u>

* <u>LFTs</u>

* <u>Lipase</u>, <u>amylase</u>

* Blood <u>type and screen</u>

* <u>ESR</u>/<u>CRP</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* <u>β-hCG</u> urine test

* Cultures





> [!TIP]
> Strongly consider a urine <u>pregnancy test</u> in sexually active female patients of reproductive age, irrespective of current <u>contraception</u> use.




> [!TIP]
> Patients with obvious signs of diffuse <u>peritonitis</u> or <u>sepsis</u> may require immediate surgical management without further diagnostic imaging.




### Imaging [[8]](/library/GKYB3J)[[9]](/library/p8XLn-)[[10]](/library/s6YtmJ)[[11]](/library/doYoaJ)[[12]](/library/jJY_FJ)[[13]](/library/CIYqUq)[[14]](/library/YGYnBq)




#### Approach




* The initial imaging modality should be guided by the working diagnosis, as based on the <u>patient history</u>, <u>vital signs</u>, and examination.

* The following recommendations apply to nonpregnant adults.

* In pregnant women with acute abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>ultrasound</u> and/or <u>MRI</u> of the abdomen and/or <u>pelvis</u> without contrast are the preferred initial imaging modalities.





#### By suspected diagnosis [[11]](/library/doYoaJ)




| Suspected diagnosis | Recommended imaging modality |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u> | <br><br>* <u>ECG</u><br><br>* <u>TTE</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Hemorrhagic shock</u> [[12]](/library/jJY_FJ)<br> | <br>* <u>FAST</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Bowel perforation</u> [[8]](/library/GKYB3J)<br> | <br><br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast<br><br>* <u>X-ray abdomen</u> (upright and <u>supine</u>) with <u>x-ray chest</u> (upright)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Small bowel obstruction</u> [[9]](/library/p8XLn-)<br> |  |
| <u>Intraabdominal abscess</u> | <br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast<br><br> |
| <br>Acute <u>diverticulitis</u> [[13]](/library/CIYqUq)<br> |  |
| <br><u>Acute appendicitis</u> [[10]](/library/s6YtmJ)<br> |  |
| <br><u>Acute mesenteric ischemia</u> [[15]](/library/XGY9Bq)<br> | <br>* <u>CTA</u> of the abdomen<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute pancreatitis</u> [[16]](/library/bGYHBq)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> abdomen<br><br>* CT abdomen with IV contrast<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Nephrolithiasis</u> [[17]](/library/yIYd2q)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u><br><br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> without contrast  [[17]](/library/yIYd2q)[[18]](/library/cAcaiU0)[[19]](/library/1Ac2iU0)<br><br><br> |

> [!TIP]
> Maintain a low threshold for obtaining diagnostic imaging in older patients, for whom abdominal <u>pain</u> is associated with higher <u>morbidity</u> and mortality as well as lower initial diagnostic <u>accuracy</u>. [[23]](/library/YxcnEe0)




> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>diagnostic laparoscopy</u> in hemodynamically stable patients in which the diagnosis is still unclear after complete <u>physical examination</u> and imaging. For patients with <u>hemodynamic instability</u> or severe abdominal distention, proceed to diagnostic <u>laparotomy</u>. [[24]](/library/UJYbtJ)




> [!TIP]
> In pregnant patients, regardless of the site of <u>pain</u>, <u>ultrasound</u> and <u>MRI</u> are the preferred initial imaging modalities.

## Cardiovascular causes

| <u>Cardiovascular causes of acute abdominal pain</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Diagnostic findings | Acute management |
| <br><u>Acute coronary syndrome</u> [[25]](/library/tbYXvn)[[26]](/library/OnYItp)<br> | <br><br>* Heavy, dull, pressure/squeezing sensation<br><br>* Substernal or epigastric <u>pain</u> with radiation to left shoulder<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* <u>Diaphoresis</u>, <u>anxiety</u><br><br>* <u>Dizziness</u>, <u>lightheadedness</u>, <u>syncope</u><br><br>* <u>Pain</u> may improve with <u>nitroglycerin</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ECG</u>: nonspecific changes, <u>ST-segment elevation</u>/<u>depression</u>, <u>T-wave inversions</u>, <u>Q waves</u><br><br>* Increased or normal <u>troponin</u><br><br>* <u>TTE</u>: hypokinesis, regional wall motion abnormalities<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for STEMI</u>” and “<u>Acute management checklist for NSTEMI/UA</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute mesenteric ischemia</u><br> [[27]](/library/ZrYZfq)[[28]](/library/0rYefq)[[29]](/library/aqYQCJ)[[30]](/library/XqY9CJ)<br> | <br><br>* Age > 60 years, embolic <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>thrombophilia</u>), cardiovascular disease<br><br>* <u>Pain out of proportion</u> to findings<br><br>* Severe, <u>diffuse abdominal pain</u> and distention<br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u><br><br>* <u>Melena</u>, <u>hematochezia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs: <u>lactic acidosis</u>, <u>hyperkalemia</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray abdomen</u>: normal (early stages), <u>pneumatosis intestinalis</u> (late stages)<br><br>* <u>CT angiography</u>: <u>mesenteric</u> arterial narrowing or occlusion, thickening of bowel wall, nonenhancing segments of solid organs or of the bowel wall, <u>pneumatosis intestinalis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute mesenteric ischemia</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Ruptured AAA</u> (or impending rupture) [[31]](/library/4JY38J)<br> | <br><br>* Age > 50 years<br><br>* Sudden, severe central abdominal, chest, and/or <u>back pain</u><br><br>* <u>Hypotension</u>, <u>shock</u><br><br>* Pulsatile mass in the midline of the abdomen<br><br>* <u>Grey Turner sign</u> and/or <u>Cullen sign</u><br><br>* History of <u>atherosclerosis</u>, <u>hypertension</u>, and/or smoking<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Imaging is only recommended in hemodynamically-stable patients with a low <u>pretest probability</u> of <u>ruptured AAA</u>.<br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: aortic dilatation, periaortic fluid, <u>intraperitoneal</u> free fluid (See also “<u>POCUS for suspected AAA</u>.”)<br><br>* CT/<u>MR angiography</u>: retro- and <u>intraperitoneal</u> hemorrhage; localization of the ruptured/leaking site<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for ruptured AAA</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Aortic dissection</u>  [[32]](/library/P6YWOJ)[[33]](/library/mM0V6g)[[34]](/library/D8Y1KI)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden onset of severe, sharp tearing chest or abdominal <u>pain</u> that radiates to the back<br><br>* <u>Hypotension</u>, <u>syncope</u>, neurological symptoms<br><br>* Asymmetrical blood pressure, <u>pulse deficit</u><br><br>* New <u>diastolic</u> <u>murmur</u> (due to <u>aortic regurgitation</u>)<br><br>* Symptoms of <u>myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Elevated <u>D-dimer</u><br><br>* <u>ECG</u>: nonspecific <u>ST-segment</u> changes<br><br>* <u>CXR</u>: widening of the aorta<br><br>* <u>CT angiography</u> of chest/abdomen/<u>pelvis</u>: <u>intimal flap</u> with false lumen<br><br>* <u>Transesophageal echocardiography</u> (<u>TEE</u>): <u>proximal aortic dissection</u>, tamponade, <u>aortic regurgitation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for aortic dissection</u>.”<br><br> |

## Gastrointestinal causes

| <u>Gastrointestinal causes of acute abdomen</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Diagnostic findings | Acute management |
| <br><u>GI tract perforation</u> [[8]](/library/GKYB3J)[[35]](/library/guYFqI)[[36]](/library/SuYyqI)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden onset of <u>diffuse abdominal pain</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* <u>Constipation</u>/<u>obstipation</u><br><br>* Diffuse <u>abdominal guarding</u>, rigidity, and <u>rebound tenderness</u><br><br>* Absent <u>bowel sounds</u><br><br>* Loss of <u>liver</u> dullness on <u>RUQ</u> percussion<br><br><br> | <br>* Abdominal <u>x-ray</u>: <u>pneumoperitoneum</u><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for GI tract perforation</u>” and “<u>Acute management checklist for esophageal perforation</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Mechanical bowel obstruction</u> [[8]](/library/GKYB3J)[[9]](/library/p8XLn-)[[37]](/library/OLYIBp)[[38]](/library/PLYWBp)<br> | <br><br>* Colicky abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Obstipation</u>/<u>bloating</u><br><br>* Progressive <u>nausea and vomiting</u> (late finding)<br><br>* Diffuse abdominal distention, tympanic abdomen, collapsed <u>rectum</u> on <u>DRE</u><br><br>* Tinkling <u>bowel sounds</u><br><br>* History of abdominal <u>surgery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>X-ray abdomen</u> <br><br>* Dilated bowel loops <u>proximal</u> to the obstruction<br><br>* Rectal air shadow absent<br><br>* Multiple air-fluid levels<br><br>* CT abdomen with IV contrast <br><br>* Similar findings as on <u>x-ray</u><br><br>* Transition point at site of obstruction<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for mechanical bowel obstruction</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute appendicitis</u> (including <u>perforated appendicitis</u>) [[39]](/library/7KY43J)[[40]](/library/v6YA5J)[[41]](/library/69Yjor)[[42]](/library/p9YLor)<br> | <br><br>* <u>RLQ</u>, epigastric, and/or periumbilical <u>pain</u> (migrating abdominal <u>pain</u>)<br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>anorexia</u><br><br>* Guarding, tenderness, and <u>rebound tenderness</u> in the <u>RLQ</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neutrophilic leukocytosis</u><br><br>* Abdominal <u>CT scan</u> with IV contrast  : distended <u>appendix</u> with periappendiceal <u>fat stranding</u><br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasonography</u> : noncompressible, aperistaltic, distended <u>appendix</u>, probe tenderness in the <u>RLQ</u>, <u>Target sign</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute appendicitis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Peptic ulcer disease</u> [[43]](/library/m8YVMI)[[44]](/library/LuYw7I)[[45]](/library/TBa6ZM)<br> | <br><br>* Epigastric <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Duodenal ulcer</u>: <u>pain</u> relieved with food; weight gain<br><br>* <u>Gastric ulcer</u>: <u>pain</u> exacerbated by food; weight loss<br><br>* Signs of <u>GI bleed</u><br><br>* History of <u>NSAID</u> intake<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anemia</u>, positive <u>FOBT</u> (in cases of bleeding <u>ulcer</u>)<br><br>* <u>Urea breath test</u> for <u>H. pylori</u>: positive in most cases of <u>PUD</u><br><br>* <u>EGD</u>: <u>Mucosal</u> <u>erosions</u> and/or <u>ulcers</u> are required for a definitive diagnosis.<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for peptic ulcer disease</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Diverticulitis</u> [[46]](/library/pJYLEJ)[[47]](/library/IJYYvJ)[[48]](/library/T8Y6NI)[[49]](/library/jR0_5f)[[50]](/library/S8YyNI)[[51]](/library/h8YcmI)[[52]](/library/x9YEpr)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Constipation</u><br><br>* Tender mass in <u>LLQ</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs: ↑ <u>WBC</u><br><br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast: <u>colonic diverticula</u> with pericolic <u>mesenteric</u> <u>fat stranding</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for diverticulitis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Gastroenteritis</u> [[53]](/library/xMYEIp)<br> | <br><br>* Abdominal cramping<br><br>* <u>Diarrhea</u>, <u>nausea</u>, and/or <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Mild cases: normal <u>abdominal examination</u><br><br>* Severe cases: abdominal tenderness, <u>fever</u>, <u>dehydration</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Diagnostic studies typically not required<br><br>* <u>CBC</u> and <u>BMP</u> can be considered for <u>severe gastroenteritis</u> or in patients with <u>risk factors</u> for severe illness<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for infectious gastroenteritis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br>Neutropenic enterocolitis (<u>typhlitis</u>) [[54]](/library/gBXFZ00)[[55]](/library/Xxc9Ee0)[[56]](/library/5xciCe0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* Bloody <u>diarrhea</u><br><br>* <u>RLQ</u> <u>pain</u><br><br>* Presence of oral or anal <u>mucosal</u> inflammation.  [[57]](/library/Txc6De0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: <u>neutropenia</u><br><br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast <br><br>* Cecal distention<br><br>* Cecal wall thickening<br><br>* <u>Pneumatosis intestinalis</u><br><br>* <u>Mesenteric</u> stranding<br><br>* Pericolic fluid<br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasonography</u>  [[58]](/library/bxcHEe0)<br><br>* Findings similar to <u>CT scan</u><br><br>* Absent <u>peristalsis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Empiric <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u><br><br>* Bowel rest<br><br>* <u>IV fluid therapy</u><br><br>* Consult <u>surgery</u> if there are signs of:<br><br>* <u>Bowel perforation</u><br><br>* Persistent <u>GI bleeding</u><br><br>* Clinical deterioration with medical management alone<br><br>* See also “<u>Management of neutropenic fever</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <br><br>Epiploic appendagitis  [[59]](/library/gxcFDe0)[[60]](/library/SxcyDe0)<br> | <br>* Lower abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: typically normal<br><br>* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast<br><br>* Ovoid lesion of fat density with high-density rim adjacent to the <u>colon</u><br><br>* Localized <u>fat stranding</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Self-limited</u>; can be treated with <u>NSAIDs</u><br><br> |

## Biliary and pancreatic causes

| <u>Biliary and pancreatic causes of acute abdomen</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Diagnostic findings | Acute management |
| <br><u>Acute pancreatitis</u> [[61]](/library/qoYC1J)[[62]](/library/MJYMuJ)[[63]](/library/HDYKfr)<br> | <br><br>* Severe epigastric <u>pain</u> that radiates to the back (circumferential <u>pain</u>)<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Epigastric tenderness, guarding, rigidity<br><br>* Hypoactive <u>bowel sounds</u><br><br>* Possibly <u>fever</u><br><br>* History of <u>gallstones</u> or <u>alcohol</u> use<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ <u>Lipase</u>, <u>amylase</u><br><br>* <u>Hypocalcemia</u> (poor prognostic indicator)<br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: <u>pancreatic</u> <u>edema</u>, peripancreatic fluid, <u>gallstones</u><br><br>* Abdominal CT with IV contrast : <u>pancreatic</u> <u>edema</u>, peripancreatic <u>fat stranding</u>, <u>gallstones</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute pancreatitis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br>Symptomatic <u>cholelithiasis</u> [[64]](/library/9lYN_6)[[65]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[66]](/library/2EYTEI)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Biliary colic</u>: <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u> with radiation to the right shoulder<br><br>* <u>Postprandial</u> onset<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Normal <u>abdominal examination</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs: normal<br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: <u>gallstones</u> with <u>posterior acoustic shadow</u><br><br>* See also “<u>POCUS for cholelithiasis</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for biliary colic</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Choledocholithiasis</u> [[64]](/library/9lYN_6)[[67]](/library/wlYh_6)<br> | <br><br>* <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u><br><br>* Features of <u>obstructive jaundice</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Normal <u>abdominal examination</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs: ↑ <u>ALP</u>, <u>AST</u>, <u>ALT</u>, total <u>bilirubin</u><br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> [[68]](/library/1EY2uI)[[69]](/library/ZvYZAI)<br><br>* Dilated <u>common bile duct</u> (<u>CBD</u>)<br><br>* Intrahepatic biliary dilatation<br><br>* Echogenic structure within the <u>CBD</u> with shadowing<br><br>* <u>EUS</u>: stone within the <u>CBD</u><br><br>* <u>MRCP</u> or <u>ERCP</u>: filling defect in the contrast-enhanced duct<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for choledocholithiasis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute cholecystitis</u> [[64]](/library/9lYN_6)[[65]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[70]](/library/5mYiTp)[[71]](/library/tMYXqp)[[72]](/library/-lYDz6)<br> | <br><br>* Severe <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u>, chills<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Right shoulder <u>referred pain</u><br><br>* <u>Murphy sign</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs: ↑ <u>WBC</u><br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> (see also “<u>Biliary POCUS</u>”): <u>sonographic Murphy sign</u> , pericholecystic fluid collection, <u>gallbladder</u> wall thickening, and/or <u>edema</u> (<u>double-wall sign</u>) [[73]](/library/bEYH8I)<br><br>* <u>HIDA scan</u> : nonvisualization of the <u>gallbladder</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute cholecystitis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute cholangitis</u> [[64]](/library/9lYN_6)[[65]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[74]](/library/TlY6w6)[[75]](/library/NrY-hq) [[70]](/library/5mYiTp)[[76]](/library/6DYj2r)[[77]](/library/DMY1Ip)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Charcot triad</u>: <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, and <u>jaundice</u><br><br>* <u>Reynold pentad</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs<br><br>* ↑ <u>WBC</u> and <u>CRP</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>ALP</u>, ↑ <u>AST</u>, ↑ <u>ALT</u>, ↑ <u>GGT</u><br><br>* ↑ Total <u>bilirubin</u><br><br>* Positive <u>blood cultures</u><br><br>* <u>RUQ</u> <u>ultrasound</u>: biliary dilation and/or evidence of obstruction (e.g., <u>choledocholithiasis</u>), thickening of <u>bile</u> duct walls<br><br>* <u>MRCP</u>/<u>ERCP</u>  : findings similar to those on <u>ultrasound</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute cholangitis</u>.”<br><br> |

| <u>Genitourinary causes of acute abdominal pain</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Diagnostic findings | Acute management |
| <br><u>Ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u> [[78]](/library/vpYArJ)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden severe lower abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Vaginal bleeding</u> or <u>amenorrhea</u><br><br>* Lower <u>abdominal guarding</u> and tenderness<br><br>* <u>Cervical motion tenderness</u>, closed <u>cervix</u><br><br>* Enlarged <u>uterus</u><br><br>* <u>Tachycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ <u>β-hCG</u><br><br>* Transabdominal/<u>transvaginal ultrasound</u><br><br>* Free fluid within <u>Morison pouch</u>   and/or <u>pouch of Douglas</u> (See also “<u>FAST scan</u>” in “<u>POCUS</u>.”)<br><br>* Empty <u>uterine cavity</u>, thickened <u>endometrial</u> lining<br><br>* <u>Adnexal mass</u><br><br>* <u>Tubal ring sign</u><br><br>* For the <u>ultrasound</u> technique, see “<u>POCUS for early pregnancy</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for ectopic pregnancy</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Ruptured ovarian cyst</u> [[79]](/library/0gbeFG)[[80]](/library/agbQFG)[[81]](/library/MbbM8H) [[82]](/library/AN1Rdh0)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden-onset unilateral lower abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Peritonitis</u><br><br>* <u>Clinical features of shock</u> (in case of significant hemorrhage)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Transabdominal/<u>transvaginal ultrasound</u>: free fluid in the <u>pouch of Douglas</u> [[83]](/library/JbbsuH)<br><br>* CT <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast: <u>pelvic</u> <u>hemoperitoneum</u> [[84]](/library/ZTbZ6G)<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for ruptured ovarian cyst</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Ovarian torsion</u> [[85]](/library/NJY-8J)[[86]](/library/E9Y86r)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden onset unilateral lower abdominal or <u>pelvic pain</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Unilateral iliac fossa tenderness<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pelvic</u> (or transvaginal) <u>ultrasound</u> with Doppler velocimetry: enlarged, <u>edematous</u> <u>ovaries</u> with decreased blood flow<br><br>* <u>Pelvic</u> <u>CT scan</u> with IV contrast <br><br>* Unilateral thickened ovarian tube, enlarged <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>ovary</u>, and decreased <u>enhancement</u> of <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>ovary</u><br><br>* Twisted vascular pedicle (<u>whirlpool sign</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for ovarian torsion</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Testicular torsion</u> [[87]](/library/q50COg)<br> | <br><br>* Severe lower quadrant and testicular <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u><br><br>* Abnormally elevated position of the <u>testis</u> within the <u>scrotum</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u><br><br>* <u>Doppler ultrasound</u>: twisting of the <u>spermatic cord</u>, reduced <u>perfusion</u> of the affected <u>testicle</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for testicular torsion</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br>Acute <u>pyelonephritis</u> [[12]](/library/jJY_FJ)[[88]](/library/wRYh6K)[[89]](/library/ysYdxq)[[90]](/library/BRYz6K)[[91]](/library/zRYrpK)<br> | <br><br>* High <u>fever</u>, chills<br><br>* Flank <u>pain</u> with <u>costovertebral angle tenderness</u> (usually unilateral, may be bilateral)<br><br>* <u>Dysuria</u>, <u>urinary frequency</u>, urgency<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Labs<br><br>* ↑ <u>WBC</u>, <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u><br><br>* Positive <u>urinalysis</u><br><br>* Positive <u>urine culture</u><br><br>* <u>Renal ultrasound</u>: <u>edema</u> and focal <u>hypoechogenic</u> areas<br><br>* CT <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast:  focal area(s) of hypoenhancement that extend to the cortical periphery<br><br><br> | <br>* See the “<u>Acute management checklist for acute pyelonephritis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Nephrolithiasis</u> | <br><br>* Severe unilateral and colicky flank <u>pain</u> (<u>renal colic</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hematuria</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* <u>Dysuria</u>, frequency, and urgency<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Urine dipstick</u> and <u>urinalysis</u>: gross or <u>microscopic hematuria</u><br><br>* Urine microscopy: to detect crystals<br><br>* Abdominopelvic CT: Nonenhanced <u>CT scan</u> is the <u>gold standard</u>.<br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u>: method of choice for patients in whom radiation exposure should be minimized (e.g., pregnant patients, children, recurrent stone formers)<br><br><br> | <br>* See “Treatment”-section in “<u>Nephrolithiasis</u>.”<br><br> |
| <u>Pelvic inflammatory disease</u> | <br><br>* Recent <u>sexual activity</u><br><br>* <u>Pelvic</u> or lower abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Cervical motion tenderness</u><br><br>* Uterine tenderness<br><br>* Adnexal tenderness<br><br>* Mucopurulent cervical/<u>vaginal discharge</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> (See “<u>Diagnostic criteria for PID</u>.”)<br><br>* <u>Pregnancy test</u><br><br>* <u>NAAT</u> for <u>gonorrhea</u> and <u>chlamydia</u><br><br>* <u>Wet mount</u>: for <u>leukorrhea</u>, <u>trichomoniasis</u>, <u>bacterial vaginosis</u><br><br>* <u>HIV testing</u> and <u>syphilis testing</u><br><br>* <u>Additional evaluation for PID</u> (e.g., with <u>pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u>) if <u>tuboovarian abscess</u> is suspected<br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Treatment of PID</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br><u>Acute urinary retention</u> [[7]](/library/35YSPp)[[92]](/library/DjX1cy)[[93]](/library/6A0jki)<br> | <br><br>* Commonly seen in older men<br><br>* Painful inability to void<br><br>* Suprapubic <u>pain</u><br><br>* Palpable distended <u>bladder</u><br><br>* Restlessness and/or acute <u>distress</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Urinalysis</u> and culture: to evaluate for <u>UTI</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, and <u>glucosuria</u><br><br>* <u>BMP</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u> in cases of <u>renal failure</u> due to obstruction<br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> of <u>urinary tract</u>: <u>bladder</u> distention<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Urgent <u>bladder catheterization</u><br><br>* Urology referral for management of the underlying condition<br><br><br> |

## Treatment

Definitive treatment of abdominal <u>pain</u> is cause-specific (e.g., see “<u>Gastrointestinal causes of acute abdominal pain</u>”). Consider the following general therapies on an individual basis:




### Supportive care for acute abdominal pain




* <u>Parenteral analgesics</u>

* <u>Empiric antibiotics for intraabdominal infections</u>

* <u>Antiemetics</u>

* <u>NG tube placement</u>

* Urinary catheter placement (e.g., <u>Foley catheter</u>)





### Empiric antibiotics for intraabdominal infections




* Determine if the infection is community-acquired or healthcare-associated and how severe it is.

* Consider organisms commonly implicated in intraabdominal infection (e.g., <u>E. coli</u>).

* Consider local resistance patterns.

* See also “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for acute biliary infection</u>.”





#### <u>Community-acquired infections</u> [[94]](/library/3t0SW3)[[95]](/library/nqY7_J)[[96]](/library/LqYw_J)




* Consider coverage of the following organisms:

* <u>Enteric</u> gram-positive <u>streptococci</u>

* <u>Enteric</u> gram-negative aerobic and facultative <u>bacilli</u>

* <u>Fluoroquinolone</u>-resistant <u>E. coli</u>

* <u>Enterococcal</u> coverage is not usually necessary for mild to moderate <u>community-acquired infection</u> but is recommended for severe infection.

* <u>Fluoroquinolones</u> are only recommended as a single-agent regimen if the hospital <u>antibiogram</u> indicates > 90% susceptibility of <u>E. coli</u>. [[94]](/library/3t0SW3)





| Severity of infection | <br>Suggested single-agent empiric regimen [[94]](/library/3t0SW3)<br> | <br>Suggested combination empiric regimen [[94]](/library/3t0SW3)<br> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Mild or moderate infection<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cefoxitin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ertapenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Moxifloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Tigecycline</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ticarcillin/clavulanate</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Metronidazole</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* PLUS one of the following<br><br>* <u>Cefazolin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Cefotaxime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Cefuroxime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| <br>Severe infection<br>and/or<br>high-risk patient<br> | <br><br>* <u>Doripenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Imipenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Piperacillin/tazobactam</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Metronidazole</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* PLUS one of the following<br><br>* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Metronidazole</u> is contraindicated in the <u>first trimester</u> of <u>pregnancy</u>.




#### <u>Healthcare-associated infections</u> [[70]](/library/5mYiTp)[[94]](/library/3t0SW3)[[95]](/library/nqY7_J)[[96]](/library/LqYw_J)




<u>Healthcare-associated infections</u> are more likely to be <u>antibiotic</u>-resistant. Consider institutional <u>antibiograms</u> when choosing an empiric regimen.




* Consider coverage of the following organisms:

* <u>Enteric</u> gram-positive <u>streptococci</u>

* <u>Enteric</u> gram-negative aerobic and anaerobic <u>bacilli</u> (including <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u>)

* <u>Enterococci</u>

* <u>MRSA</u>

* Agents to avoid as empiric therapy

* <u>Cephalosporins</u> as a single-agent regimen

* <u>Fluoroquinolones</u> as a single-agent regimen

* <u>Ampicillin-sulbactam</u>





| <br>Patient and/or institutional <u>risk factors</u><br><br> | <br>Suggested empiric regimens [[94]](/library/3t0SW3)<br> |
| --- | --- |
| <br>Low risk (< 20%) of infection with resistant organism <br><br> | <br>* 1) Single-agent regimen<br><br>* <u>Carbapenems</u><br><br>* <u>Doripenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Imipenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>piperacillin/tazobactam</u> DOSAGE<br><br> |
| <br>* 2) Combination regimen<br><br>* <u>Metronidazole</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* PLUS one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE<br><br> |  |
| <br>High risk (> 20%) of infection with resistant organism <br> | <br>* Single-agent or combination empiric regimen (see above) PLUS one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Aminoglycoside</u><br><br>* <u>Gentamicin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Tobramycin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Amikacin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR <u>polymyxin</u> DOSAGE  [[95]](/library/nqY7_J) [[97]](/library/-IYD2q)<br><br>* OR a new combination <u>beta-lactam</u><br><br>* <u>Ceftolozane/tazobactam</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ceftazidime</u>/avibactam DOSAGE<br><br> |
| <br>High risk of <u>MRSA</u>  <br> | <br><br>* Combination empiric regimen (see above)<br><br>* PLUS <u>vancomycin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Obtain cultures, if necessary, before the administration of empirical IV <u>antibiotics</u>.




> [!TIP]
> For patients with a <u>beta-lactam</u> or <u>carbapenem</u> <u>allergy</u>, consider <u>vancomycin</u> with <u>aztreonam</u> and <u>metronidazole</u>.




### <u>Surgery</u>




* The definitive management of most causes of acute abdomen is surgical.

* The choice of procedure and the urgency of <u>surgery</u> is determined by the underlying condition.

* Patients with signs of diffuse <u>peritonitis</u> or <u>sepsis</u> require immediate surgical management, which should not be delayed by time-consuming diagnostic tests.

* Examples of urgent consultations:

* General <u>surgery</u> for <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients with a rigid abdomen

* Vascular <u>surgery</u> for a ruptured or symptomatic <u>AAA</u>

* <u>OB/GYN</u> for a <u>ruptured ectopic pregnancy</u>

| <u>RUQ</u> | <br><br>* <u>Biliary colic</u><br><br>* <u>Acute cholecystitis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute cholangitis</u><br><br>* <u>Emphysematous cholecystitis</u><br><br>* Acute <u>hepatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Pyogenic liver abscess</u><br><br>* <u>Duodenal ulcer</u><br><br>* <u>Portal vein thrombosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Lower lobe <u>pneumonia</u><br><br>* Lower lobe <u>pulmonary infarction</u> (<u>pulmonary embolism</u>)<br><br>* <u>Empyema</u><br><br>* <u>Ureteric colic</u><br><br>* <u>Pyelonephritis</u><br><br><br> |

| <u>RLQ</u> | <br><br>* <u>Acute appendicitis</u><br><br>* <u>Colitis</u><br><br>* <u>IBD</u><br><br>* <u>Epiploic appendagitis</u><br><br>* <u>Neutropenic enterocolitis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ureteric colic</u> (<u>nephrolithiasis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ectopic pregnancy</u><br><br>* <u>Ovarian torsion</u><br><br>* <u>Ruptured ovarian cyst</u><br><br>* <u>PID</u><br><br>* <u>Testicular torsion</u><br><br><br> |

| Epigastrium | <br><br>* Acute <u>esophagitis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute gastritis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute pancreatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute mesenteric ischemia</u><br><br>* <u>PUD</u><br><br>* <u>GERD</u><br><br>* <u>Functional dyspepsia</u><br><br>* <u>Mallory Weiss syndrome</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Myocardial infarction</u><br><br>* <u>Pericarditis</u><br><br>* <u>AAA</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u><br><br><br> |
| Periumbilical | <br><br>* <u>Acute appendicitis</u> (early)<br><br>* <u>Mesenteric</u> <u>ischemia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>AAA</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u><br><br><br> |
